name: Cash Flow Forecasting
title: Cash Flow Forecasting
answer: Cash flow forecasting covers the projection of cash receipts and payments across defined time horizons, from intraday balances to weekly, monthly, and quarterly views. It spans operating cash flows such as customer collections, supplier payments, payroll, and tax, as well as financing and investing flows like debt service, interest, capital expenditure, and intercompany transfers. Forecasts are usually built by legal entity, bank account, currency, and business unit, and they support liquidity planning, funding decisions, and working capital management. The scope also includes scenario and sensitivity analysis, because actual cash timing rarely matches a single deterministic plan.

It spans operating cash flows such as customer collections, supplier payments, payroll, and tax, as well as financing and investing flows like debt service, interest, capital expenditure, and intercompany transfers. sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on data pulled from ERP systems, treasury management systems, accounts receivable and payable subledgers, bank statement feeds, payment gateways, and market data services. These sources are connected through APIs, file transfers, or scheduled extracts into a data warehouse, a treasury database, or a planning platform. Spreadsheets remain common at the edges, but production forecasting typically uses a governed pipeline with data validation, mapping tables, and refresh schedules. Dashboards and reporting layers then present forecast versus actual positions to treasury, finance, and business teams.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start by cleaning and aligning historical cash data, then map transactions to drivers such as invoice terms, payment behavior, seasonality, and contractual dates. Statistical and machine learning models, including time series methods, regression, and classification, produce baseline forecasts, while rules and driver-based models handle known commitments. Backtesting and variance analysis compare predictions with actual cash movements, and forecasters adjust for one-off items, payment runs, and holiday effects. The output is often a probabilistic range rather than a single number, with human review before it feeds liquidity decisions.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance: Cash flow forecasts depend on sensitive bank, customer, and supplier data, so access controls, encryption, and segregation of duties are central. Provenance requires clear lineage from source system to transformed feature to final forecast, with timestamps, version history, and documented assumptions. Model risk management practices include validation, performance monitoring, and limits on automated adjustments, especially where forecasts influence funding or hedging. Audit trails and reconciliation controls help satisfy internal and external reporting requirements, and third-party data or model providers need contractual clarity on use, retention, and liability.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going: Forecasting is moving toward more frequent, sometimes intraday, cycles as bank APIs and real-time payment rails become more common. Probabilistic and scenario-based outputs are replacing single-point plans in many treasury teams, and automation is reducing manual spreadsheet work. Generative and conversational interfaces may help explain variances and draft commentary, but the underlying numbers still require validation. The direction is tighter integration between ERP, treasury, and planning systems, with governance and explainability keeping pace.
